The consensus among ophthalmic pathology and basic science research studies is that SBK (Sub-Bowman's Keratomileusis) and ASA (Advanced Surface Ablation) are improvements in excimer laser keratorefractive surgery compared to conventional LASIK or PRK, particularly with regard to maintaining corneal biomechanics. Studies have shown that SBK tends to preserve the cornea's natural shape and structure more effectively than traditional surface ablation techniques like ASA.

Advanced Surface Ablation (ASA), also known as "surface-only" excimer keratectomy, involves removing only the outermost layer of the cornea without reshaping its underlying tissue. While ASA has improved significantly over time, it is not considered a fully effective alternative to traditional LASIK or PRK in maintaining corneal biomechanics.

In contrast, SBK typically preserves more of the natural corneal structure and function, which can lead to better long-term outcomes for patients. A study published in the Journal of Refractive Surgery found that SBK resulted in improved corneal wavefront aberrations compared to traditional surface ablation techniques like ASA.

However, it's essential to note that wound healing issues are still present after excimer laser keratorefractive surgery, and both SBK and ASA may contribute to this issue. Ophthalmic pathology research suggests that the duration of inflammation and healing can affect the outcome of surgical procedures, with longer durations potentially increasing the risk of complications.

In summary, while there is no clear consensus on whether advanced surface ablation or sub-Bowman's keratomileusis is more effective in maintaining corneal biomechanics after excimer laser keratorefractive surgery, the available evidence suggests that SBK is generally considered a better option than ASA. Nevertheless, wound healing issues are still an area of ongoing research and may require further investigation to optimize surgical outcomes for patients undergoing these procedures.
